model.name: SDM-1
model.one_line: A foundation model for experiment design in biotech, biochemical and chemical development: it reads a campaign's results so far and proposes which experiments to run next.

model_details.inputs: The campaign so far: parameter settings and measured outcomes, plus declared outcome limits (a floor where runs fail, a ceiling where a readout saturates)
outputs: A full predictive distribution of the outcome at any untested setting
The probability that a run succeeds
Proposals for the next experiment or the next batch

intended_use: Choosing the next experiments in biotech, biochemical and chemical campaigns where each experiment is expensive: formulation, media and buffer optimization, assay development, reaction conditions, protocol and process parameters
Ranking a candidate list (for example a plate of untested formulations) by expected outcome
Campaigns that aim for a target value, stay within limits, or trade off several outcomes

capabilities.name: Batches
capabilities.text: Proposes a whole batch at once, from 1 to [MAX BATCH] experiments.

capabilities.name: Targets, not just maxima
capabilities.text: Aim for a value (for example 50% yield within a tolerance) and get the probability of landing in range.

capabilities.name: Failed runs and saturated readouts
capabilities.text: Declare where runs fail or a readout saturates; the model reads those results as limits, not exact values.

capabilities.name: Limits on other outcomes
capabilities.text: Keep cost, purity or other measured outcomes within limits while optimizing one.

capabilities.name: Several objectives
capabilities.text: See the trade-off between competing outcomes and choose where to sit on it.

capabilities.name: Mixed parameter types
capabilities.text: Continuous, integer, log-scale and categorical parameters.

capabilities.name: No per-campaign tuning
capabilities.text: Nothing is fitted or tuned per campaign: the model reads the history and predicts directly.

enables.title: Every plate ranked
enables.text: A team screening one plate a week gets the next plate proposed and every candidate ranked, so reagent goes to the wells most likely to win or to teach the most.

enables.title: Failed runs count as information
enables.text: Campaigns where many conditions fail (precipitation, no growth, no signal) or a readout saturates can declare those limits instead of hiding or deleting the runs.

enables.title: Aim for a value, not just the maximum
enables.text: Hitting 50% yield within a tolerance, or a viscosity window, is a goal in its own right, with the probability of landing in range for every proposal.

enables.title: No modeling expertise per campaign
enables.text: There is no model to fit, kernel to choose or setting to tune: the lab supplies its results so far and gets the next experiments.

enables.title: From a few parameters to many
enables.text: The same model serves a two-factor optimization and a formulation with dozens of components, mixing continuous and categorical parameters.

category_explainer.title: What is a foundation model for experiment design?
category_explainer.text: Classical design of experiments plans a screen up front. Bayesian optimization fits a new statistical model to every campaign and starts from scratch each time. A foundation model for experiment design arrives ready: it already knows how lab results tend to depend on settings, from smooth trends to sharp optima, thresholds and failed runs. Given a lab's results so far, it predicts how untested settings will turn out and proposes the next experiments in seconds.

campaign_trace.problem: Ackley function, 4 parameters, with many local optima: a typical campaign, the median of 10. By experiment 25 SDM-1 had closed nearly half the gap, ahead of every other method, and after 50 it ended closest, while random search had barely moved.
campaign_trace.y_label: Gap to the best possible result (lower is better)

asides.title: How it works
asides.text: Given a campaign's results so far, SDM-1 predicts untested settings in a single pass: a full distribution over the outcome and the chance the run succeeds, with no model to fit or tune. It then proposes the settings with the most to gain.

asides.title: How these benchmarks were run
asides.text: Every method started from the same initial experiments on the same seeds and ran through the same test setup. Industry tools ran with their default settings. Every benchmark was held out of training.

faq.q: Does it need my historical data?
faq.a: No. It is ready for a new campaign from the first results. Earlier results from the same campaign make its next proposals better.

faq.q: How many parameters can a campaign have?
faq.a: Up to 100 per campaign: continuous, integer, log-scale and categorical parameters.

faq.q: Can it aim for a specific range of values instead of a maximum or minimum?
faq.a: Yes. Set a target with a tolerance and it proposes the settings most likely to land in range.
faq.was: Yes. Set a target with a tolerance and it proposes the settings most likely to land in range, with that probability for each. (until 17 Nov 2026: without ", with that probability for each")

benchmarks.source: Parsaee et al., Bioinformatics 2026, doi 10.5281/zenodo.21501659 (code CC BY 4.0); data Kim and Audet, Commun Biol 2, 48 (2019), under its own open-access article. Attribution required.
benchmarks.provenance: biofoundrydemo-ai-09, 16 Nov 2026: H1 (gamma_s1-003-037-feashead-s1, harness model-ei-body) vs GP BO (gp-ts), random as the score's reference; study 20261116-s1-003-057-media-aws, commit 41e564f. T cell (535 formulations, 14 components) and TF-1 (1562, 15); 10 seeds, 10 random initial formulations, budget 50, batch 1. Score 26.9 vs 11.9 at 25, 56.8 vs 34.5 at 50 (shown rounded; vs_bo from the unrounded). Exact (biofoundrydemo-ai-09, 16 Nov 2026): score 26.9370 vs 11.9313 at 25, 56.8136 vs 34.4840 at 50; distance 5.4563 vs 6.7388 at 25 (1.2351), 1.9947 vs 3.1332 at 50 (1.5707); top 1% 40.0 vs 40.0, 90.0 vs 85.0. Held out: H1 trained on synthetic families and own simulators only, weights 2026-11-05, these data converted 2026-11-16.
caveats: Six datasets in the paper, two shown. Inclusion rule fixed before any score: the budget covers at most 10% of the pool (T cell 9%, TF-1 3%; the other four 15% to 27%). On the other four no method beats random, GP BO included (26 to 29 components, budget a quarter of the smallest pools, best-vs-second gap below the repeat spread): a property of the benchmarks.
The score is a ratio against random, which does badly on these two pools, so it amplifies: in absolute terms the regret gap is about 1.2 points of the range at 25 and 1.1 at 50.
Per task: one better by 1 to 2%, one level, none better by more than 2%. Seed by seed, TF-1 at 50 is a tie (better on 3 of 10, worse on 3); T cell leans ahead (better on 5, worse on 2).
No TabPFN comparison yet (rerunning). 10 seeds accepted by the user after caveats 2 and 3.
Both datasets from one study by one group: not two independent pieces of evidence.
Mammalian cell-culture media optimization: never call it a biofoundry or protein-expression result.
Public academic benchmark on recorded measurements, not ProviGen lab data; the claim is sample efficiency against GP BO on the same data and seeds.

Distance per task (>2% / 1-2% / <1% of range): n=25 better 6 (4 resolved) + 1, level 6, worse 1 (p3ht_cnt_conductivity); n=50 better 5 (3), level 8, worse 1 (resolved, p3ht_cnt_conductivity). caveats: Adapted definitions (a learned oracle, no candidate set, no known optimum): optimum = best value known (max over 200,000 uniform latent-cube rows decoded by RECOB's mapping, all 2,800 published runs and ours); bottom = landscape minimum; distance = (optimum - best so far) / range; score = 100(1 - min(1, distance / random's distance)) per task, then mean; top 1% = the oracle's 99th percentile over the uniform sample (by volume). Random reaches it in 18.9% / 37.1% at 25 / 50.

Under a 2 SE rule nothing resolves at suite level: n=25 score and distance at 1.96 and 1.87 SE (borderline), n=50 level on all three. Weaker than EDBO and Liang; a separate row, never pooled into Chemistry and materials (different definitions).

top1.explain: Share of campaigns whose best result is among the best 1% of the task's candidate experiments. Higher is better.
top1.explain_brief: Share of campaigns that reach the best 1% of candidate experiments: higher is better.

benchmark_overview_added.n_note: Results are averaged over 5 to 50 runs per benchmark, typically 10. Every method on a benchmark starts from the same initial experiments, a property of the benchmark, from 2 to 12 based on published protocols where available. The number is fixed once per benchmark.
benchmark_overview_added.bo_note: Bayesian optimization: BoTorch's standard Gaussian-process model (version 0.16.1) with Thompson sampling, refitted every round. On every benchmark it runs under the same conditions as SDM-1. Thompson sampling was chosen because benchmarks of recorded experiments require choosing from a fixed list of candidates.

model_card_text.one_line: SDM-1 is ProviGen's foundation model for sequential experiment design. As a campaign progresses, it learns from each round of results and proposes the next experiments to run.
intended_use: Choosing the next experiments when each one is costly in materials, time or compute
Ranking a list of untested candidates by expected outcome
Reaching a target value, staying within limits, or balancing several outcomes
model_card_text.evaluation_summary: Standard optimization functions and published campaigns in biology, chemistry, materials, machine learning and engineering design. None of them were seen in training.
model_card_text.inputs: The parameter space and the campaign's completed experiments (settings and measured outcomes), with optional outcome limits: a failure threshold and a saturation ceiling.
outputs: Proposal for the next run: settings for the next n experiments, where n is the batch size
